subject: snail
pitch: A garden snail on an adventure. A glossy spiral shell striped in caramel, chocolate and cream, a soft grey-green body with a pebbly texture and a slimy shine, two long eye stalks with little black eyes and two short feelers below. A tiny ladybird hitches a ride on top of the shell.
reasoning:
I'm sketching out the snail's proportions and planning a skeleton with a root body joint and a spine chain running from tail to head.

Now I'm defining the eye stalks, jaw joints, and body geometry: sweeping the spine chain with a tapered radius for a flattened wide foot, and planning a mottled scaly paint scheme with adjustable roughness for a slimy sheen.

I'm working out the foot sole as a flattened strip beneath the body, adjusting the body and head sweep radii so the neck lifts naturally while the lower fringe stays grounded, then moving on to building the spiral shell.

For the shell, I'm using a planar spiral swept in the YZ plane with tube radius growing from a tight center (0.006) out to 0.022 across about 2.5 turns, giving it that conical garden-snail coil look.

I'm tuning the tube radius growth (0.004 to around 0.019) and overall shell diameter (roughly 0.074-0.085) so the shell sits naturally on the body, positioning its center around y=0.045 so it sinks slightly behind the body at z=-0.015.

For the spiral itself, I'm defining it with a starting radius near 0.004 that grows to r1, oriented around the x-axis so the whorl ends facing forward (+z), matching the aperture position where the shell opening meets the body underneath.

I'm working out the ending angle so the whorl terminates near the front-lower part of the shell—settling on roughly 2.15 turns plus a small x-axis pitch to give it a bit of helical advance rather than keeping it flat.

I realize a planar spiral with growing radius risks the tube overlapping itself if it's too thick—computing that at a radius growth of about 2.4x per turn, the gap between whorls limits the tube to roughly 0.3 times the radius, which gets quite thin toward the outer end. Real shells solve this by letting whorls overlap each other, wrapping over the previous turn rather than staying separated.

Actually, snail shell stripes run along the spiral following the whorl, so I should band colors by angle around the tube cross-section rather than along its length, cycling caramel, chocolate, and cream with some noise for a hand-painted feel, using continuous angle values from the surface coordinates.

I also want to add a cream-colored lip near the aperture by marking the last few percent of the shell length. For the shape itself, I'm defining the shell as a bone-driven sweep with a radius function that grows along the length so the tube radius matches the spiral radius at the end, giving the whorls a naturally overlapping look.

I'm realizing that with purely overlapping radii the spiral seam gets hidden entirely, so I should add a slight pitch offset per turn so the shell reads as a cone rather than a flat disc, letting the spiral be visible from the side as the camera moves around it.

I realize the sweep parameter is arc-length, not turn count, so since log-spiral arc length is roughly proportional to radius, I can approximate the tube radius as linear in t rather than exponential, scaling from about 0.003 to 0.0126, with a slight flare added near the aperture end for realism.

Now I'm working out the shell's position relative to the joint, accounting for the pitch shift along x as the spiral advances, and adjusting the shell group's center coordinates accordingly. I'm setting up the sweep call with bone attachment, tube sides, and color, then moving on to defining the body's spine path through multiple joints.

I'm adding a tip joint named "head" with a jaw joint attached for the mouth, plus small parts for the lip and jaw. For the head shape, I'm widening the tube radius near the end to form a bulge before tapering, and adjusting the path's final points so the head tilts forward and slightly upward.

Now I'm working out the width and height radius functions along the tube, using a smoothstep-based ramp so the body tapers correctly at the tail and head ends, while making sure the path's y-values line up with the radius so the bottom stays near zero.

Defining the foot sole sweep...

I'll pair darker scale shading on the back with lighter belly tones using a countershade blend, maybe adding subtle twin stripes along the back. Then I'll add eyestalks as jointed tentacle chains sprouting from the head, positioned symmetrically and curving up and outward to black sphere eye tips.

For the eye, I'll add a small bulb sphere at the stalk tip with a black eye sphere offset forward and a tiny white highlight sphere for shine, mirroring the setup across left and right sides with name suffixes. Then I'm working out feeler placements below the stalks near the head front.

Now I'm defining the mouth area at the head's front end, with an upper lip box and lower jaw box in a muted green-grey tone, plus a flattened scaled sphere for the upper jaw joint.

I'm adding the lower jaw sphere on its own hinge joint and a tiny dark mouth-slit box between the upper and lower parts, all parented to the head bone, and planning out low-poly sphere geometry helpers before placing a ladybird on the shell's top surface.

For the ladybird, I'm figuring out how to raycast from above to find the shell's top point and normal, then orient the ladybird's parts in a local frame relative to that hit point so it sits naturally on the curved surface.

Sketching the ladybird's proportions: a domed red elytra sphere scaled to form a shell, with a thin dark central stripe box placed along the top to mark the wing split, adjusting sizes so it sits naturally on the dome surface.

That gives a nice black stripe. Now I'm working out placement for small black spots on the dome surface using the ellipsoid equation to find the right height at each x,z position, plus a black sphere for the head positioned at the front.

I'm deciding to skip legs and antennae for simplicity, adding a ladybird joint attached to the shell parent, and finishing touches like the white pronotum patches and wing split line.

Now I'm working on the shell paint function, mapping angular position into color bands around the shell, but running into a seam issue where 7 bands don't divide evenly into 360 degrees—switching to 8 bands with a repeating pattern instead.

Finishing the banding pattern, I'll add a cream lip highlight near the edge, a darker chocolate tip near the apex, and subtle growth-ring darkening at regular intervals, all blended via color mixing. Then I'm setting the shell's material properties for a glossy look, adjusting roughness for the shared body surface.

For the ground trail, I'm sketching a thin, pale translucent extruded strip behind the snail in the xz-plane to suggest a slime path, working out the orientation vectors for extruding the outline along the correct normal direction.

Checking the thickness and bounding box look fine, so I'll set the color and finalize the body bone placement at the root/tail joint for a neutral mid-stride pose. Now I'm working out the eyestalk path coordinates from base to tip.

Still writing stalk geometry...

Still defining the feeler and tip geometry... I'm working out the bulb sphere placement on the chain joint, then moving on to sketch out the shell sweep surface with its ray projection for the ladybird nub details.

Now I'm positioning the shell center and tracing the spiral growth outward, figuring out where the front edge of the shell meets the body given the tube radius and the angular offset.

I'm checking that the shell's maximum back-extent and bottom clearance keep it floating safely above the ground while still looking proportionate against the body and neck, then setting up the spiral starting point for the shell geometry.

Now I'm finalizing the imports and module structure, making sure the paint utilities export correctly, and starting to write the body sweep geometry with color gradients and radius interpolation functions for the body and head shapes.

Now I'm placing the facial features on the head: eyes near the top of the head sphere, an upper and lower lip sunk slightly into the surface near the mouth, a jaw joint for articulation, and a small dark box for the mouth opening, all positioned relative to the head center and scaled to sit naturally on the body.
